Mr. Speaker, I rise on a most serious matter of privilege. The matter deals with the human rights of a Department of National Defence scientist by the name of Dr. Mendoza, and the Human Rights Commission of Canada is seized with that part of it.
The matter involves my rights as a member of Parliament because records indicate that the investigation by the Special Investigations Unit of the Department of National Defence involves telephone calls to my office, including my Prince Rupert, British Columbia, office. If members of Parliament cannot make and receive calls from the public and private, then we have lost the vital thread of our democratic freedoms.
Second, the matter involves the rights of all members of this House. One of the documents from Colonel McCullough suggests that Canadian law be violated, in fact that it be violated by the Minister of National Defence during Question Period. This cuts to the core of the operation of the most senior democratic institution of Canada.
Third, it involves the rights of all members as one of the documents revealed a view by the Department of National Defence that "the House" should not be advised of the specifics of these investigations. This view is one that challenges the basic building blocks of any parliamentary democracy.
There is a further matter involving the Department of National Defence and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, but because of the sensitivity of that part of the file it will have to be held until an in camera meeting can adjudicate upon it. Let me simply say in relation to that that it clearly violates the spirit, if not the specifics, of Canadian law.
If you will give me a moment, Mr. Speaker, I would like to put the specifics of just a few of the documents on the record because I think it will give all members of the House some idea of the severity of the question of privilege that is being raised today.
There is a document called "Chronology of Correspondence with Hon. Jim Fulton MP for Skeena concerning CB Defence Activities", and it lists the dates of letters, September 27, 1983, from Fulton to Mendoza, requesting information on teratology toxicity studies under contract on HI-6.
It then goes on, and I will not give you all of the details but it lists letters from October 11, 1983; November 29, 1983; December 19,1983; May 10,1984; and February 27, 1984. These are letters either between myself and National Defence or the minister at the time, in the case of this correspondence to Jean-Jacques Blais. The list goes on to show February 12, 1985 from myself to Dr. Mendoza and May 28, 1985.
Some of these letters were answered by the Right Hon. Joe Clark, some by the Hon. Erik Nielsen who was then Minister of National Defence, and some by the Hon. Harvie Andre who was Minister of National Defence. Some are from myself to the Hon. Jake Epp. Some are from myself to the Minister of National Defence dated August 3, 1988 and November 7, 1988, and answered by the Hon. Perrin Beatty. A letter of December 8,1988 is answered by the Hon. Perrin Beatty. A letter of December 9, 1988 from myself to the Department of National Defence was answered January 18,1989 by the Hon. Perrin Beatty. A letter of December 19, 1988 was answered April 4, 1989 by the Hon. Perrin Beatty.

subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL WOMEN'S DAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am indeed proud to rise today on the occasion of International Women's Day to make my first formal statement in this House as Canada's minister responsible for the status of women.
Traditionally, International Women's Day has been an opportunity to reflect on the progress made to advance women's equality. Indeed, there is much we can cele-

March 8, 1990

Routine Proceedings
brate in this regard. Women in Canada today have access to an unprecedented range of choices and opportunities in employment, in the roles and relationships they wish to pursue, in the lives they want to lead.

However, women know that they must remain vigilant, not only to protect the gains they have made but also to pursue the objectives that are still necessary for them to achieve equality.

The women of this country know that equality is much more than the absence of discrimination. Equality governs one's over-all well-being, one's ability to live life to the fullest. There is no such thing as equality for some; true equality means equal treatment and equal opportunities for everyone in all spheres of life. It is toward that goal of true equality that all of society must be dedicated.

The women of Canada recognize how vitally important their efforts to achieve equality are, not only to the current generation but to all generations to come.
We want the best for our children, our daughters and our sons. We want them to grow and to thrive in a society characterized by harmony and tolerance. We want our children to be free and able to find fulfilment in whatever life path they choose. At the same time, we also want the best from our children. As parents, we invest in our children's lives, not only our hopes for their individual success and achievement, but also our dreams that they in turn will take up the banner to work for the betterment of their own society and the generations that will follow them.
Let us be mindful of our Canadian society of the future as we set our sights on the new decade and the work that must be done to eliminate the remaining obstacles to women's equality.

Today we applaud the fact that women's roles and aspirations are growing and expanding at an accelerated rate.

Those in our society who are dedicated to serving women's advancement toward equality must not only keep pace but also be flexible enough to move and adapt as the goals of Canadian women change and broaden.
To respond to the challenges facing women today, new methods and new approaches are required that are based on co-operation and mutual understanding. New partnerships are required among all the parties who play a role in women's lives, partnerships involving business, organized labour, non-governmental organizations, community and voluntary groups, and all levels of government working together with women to achieve equality and a better, safer and more tolerant society.
Our government is strongly committed to women's equality. The progressive legislative changes already put in place provide a solid basis for further action. Our government will continue to work as a full partner to ensure and promote the rights of women in this country to full and equal participation in our society.

subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL WOMEN'S DAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have the honour today to speak for the Official Opposition on the status of women, on this International Women's Day.

I listened with interest to the words of the hon. minister responsible for the status of women and I congratulate her on her new responsibilities. I must say that I found it interesting as much for what she did not say as for what she did. The button that we were given before coming into the Chamber today is a shame. A black button on dark suits will not be seen anywhere in Canada. I would have thought she would have withheld this button from even being sent on.
The institutional framework which has been put into place since 1970 has facilitated progress on a wide front for women. In unprecedented numbers, women entered the paid workforce. The so-called traditional family

March 8, 1990
Routine Proceedings
mould where the man went to work while the wife stayed home with the children has been broken decisively to the point that by 1986 it applied to only 16 per cent of Canadian families.
Although individual women have achieved in the workplace and have had great successes, the status of the average woman, although improved, leaves a lot to be desired. We still have a long way to go to achieve true equality in the workplace. As long as the wages of women are lower than men, as long as women are treated as a workforce that is available at low wages in bad working conditions, we still will not have equality in the workplace. As long as women have to carry the double burden of working and taking the full responsibility for the family, we cannot have equality.
I am afraid, and I say to the minister in her position that this government's most recent budget shows just how vulnerable the silent majority in Canada is. We have seen this government begin to dismantle the institutions women have struggled so hard to put into place. Funding was almost completely eliminated for some 80 women's centres, often the first line of defence against physical and mental abuse.
Day care is still considered to be a woman's issue. Perhaps that is why this federal government felt safe to renege on its promise to enact national day care legislation. This very day we see day care workers in Halifax and across Canada striking because they are paid so little.
If we continue to allow this government to cut at the infrastructures women need, such as the Canada Assistance Program which funds day care and is being cut in three rich provinces, if we continue to see an unemployment insurance program that in many areas of the country allows women to get into the workforce to be cut back or to put a harder emphasis on it, and if we look at the employment equity bill that this minister was involved in, we will know that the condition of women has gone downhill.
We will also know that it continues to allow the simmering across Canada of impressions. We do not need ministers who continue to use women as the butt of sexist jokes, nor do we need ministers who put up with it.
I do not want to say anything about the new first for a woman minister of justice, but the abortion bill is a harsh piece of legislation for any person. It is a contestable piece of legislation. In other words, we will allow the
continued simmering across Canada of attitudes that allow violence and hate against women in the home and in the workplace. This government has to wake up to that. We cannot have situations such as that which happened at the University of Montreal.
The nicest thing that I have learned being a woman in the working world and in the world in general is that it is enjoyable to have challenges and experiences and to be able to do exactly what everybody here in this House achieved by an equal process. There were no barriers. But that is not what we see out there. We need fair play in the home and we need fair play in the workplace. We will not achieve it unless we are vigilant.
In the words of Sylvia Gold of the Advisory Council on the Status of Women:

The watchword for Canadian women in the 1990s is vigilance:
vigilance to recognize new threats to the social, economic and legal
status of women.
I do not wish to continue, but it gives the direction the government should follow and we do not see that today. We see that the status of women does not attract this government's interest.

I say to the government and the new minister that the 1990s taking us to the year 2000 will be a full challenge for this government and for all governments in Canada, and will improve the situation of the women right across Canada.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to respond to the minister's statement on International Women's Day. I am pleased to have that opportunity. In reference to some of the comments that my colleague from the Liberal party made about the button that we have today for International Women's Day, perhaps the colour of the button denotes something about the budget that this government has just brought down.
I want to congratulate the women of Canada for their dedication to achieving real equality for women. I also rise to join my voice with theirs against this government's agenda for women, which the minister barely mentioned.
The minister talked about an unprecedented range of choices for women, but she did not mention that this government is currently in the process of taking away the fundamental choice for women. With its Criminal Code

abortion law, the government is taking away the right to choose the fate of our own bodies and our own lives.
The minister talked about a partnership with voluntary groups. She failed to mentioned that core funding for over 75 voluntary women's groups has been completely withdrawn by this budget. She did not mention this government's constant attack and undermining of the women's program from Secretary of State. For the second year in a row there are big cuts to the women's program budget.
She did not mention this government's refusal to meet with the umbrella organization which represents over 600 women's groups in Canada. Will the government meet with that organization this year?
She talked about a government strongly committed to equality for women. I would like to know where is that government. It is certainly not the government that I see on the other side of this House.
The Minister did not mention that under the government's draconian economic policies the wage gap between men and women has actually increased.
She failed to state that in this budget the funding mechanism for social assistance, the Canada Assistance Plan, has been strangled for three provinces, including my province of British Columbia. This is the program that funds child care. Canada has made international commitments to the principle of child care. Canada has failed to deliver on them. This government has failed to deliver on that.
The Canada Assistance Plan funds shelters for battered women. That has been capped in three provinces in Canada. The shelters that are so desperately needed will not be provided. The minister has failed to report that this government deindexed the family allowance program and put an end to the universality of income support for mothers.
The minister said that she was proud to rise today to make her first formal statement in the House of Commons as the new Minister responsible for the Status of Women. Is she really proud of what she is saying? Is she proud of this government's shabby record on women's issues? I cannot believe it. I hope not.
Routine Proceedings
The minister talked about equality. I say and the women of Canada say that this government does not really know the meaning of the word equality. This government is attempting to silence the voices of women. Our voices will not be silenced. We will join together. Women will continue their struggle for true equality. Women will continue their struggle for social and economic justice for all in our society.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there are so many worrisome concerns that need to be addressed in this uncaring budget presented as a no-tax increase budget, which is far from forthcoming on the part of the minister or the government. It is hurtful to Canadians in need of shelter. It is hurtful to Canadians who need better education facilities and better health facilities.
My colleagues are looking at these various areas that all need careful examination and should be reconsidered. However, there are some things about this budget that are even more shameful.
There is the supposed cut in the defence budget, the absence of anything on the environment, or anything to deal with drugs, with illiteracy, with child care and today, in particular, which is International Women's Day, the cuts to women's programs, the cuts to the CAP that

March 8, 1990
The Budget
ensures a day care program-in fact the absence of day care is really a tragedy. However, I wish to focus and participate in this debate particularly looking at communications and culture. That is the perspective I would like to address.
First, let us look at native communications. Cuts to the native communications programs at the Department of the Secretary of State which account for the major cuts in that department will affect 16 native communication groups across Canada. Hardest hit and actually wiped out will be the aboriginal language newspapers, many of which have been given six months to close down their operations.
The Inuit Broadcast Corporation says that this program cut wipes out basic communication services for thousands of native Canadians living in small isolated communities. A service most Canadians take for granted is broadcasting and newspapers in their own language, something which just seems so normal. This government has sent a clear message to the founding peoples of Canada. The message is: you don't matter.
With respect to the provisions in the government's budget on the privatization of our telecommunications sector, the privatizing of Telesat Canada shows that it is still trapped in a market force ideological view. It also shows that it has failed to learn that our communications system works well because it has been carefully crafted over many decades. It works well because it all fits together.
You cannot simply remove one element, one wall from the house, without considering the whole system. This government obviously has no vision for Canada, except how to dismantle it. Petro-Canada is another example of that.
Telecommunications are just as important an economic force or an economic lever for Canada that is required and needed for us to be able to move forward into the 21st century. From this government it has been promises, promises for a national telecommunications policy for the last five years. Yet we have had no follow-up on that and no follow-up on the Supreme Court decision that would ensure that this vital sector remains in the federal domain.
However, within this vacuum the government wants to privatize Telesat, a cornerstone of our communications system, purely for profit motives and not from a public policy mandate point of view. It is disgraceful.
It is easy in difficult financial times for governments to slash expenditures on culture, to see it as an extra, as a frill. But I believe that it is in these very hard times that this sector should be supported. These products, these creations, these manifestations of expression of our inner selves need to be promoted and protected, for culture is what a country says to itself and about itself, as well as to others, whether it be through the creative medium of the theatre, film, television, novels, recorded entertainment, painting, architecture, ballet or dance. It is what makes a people interesting. It gives us a presence, a sense of worth, a sense of self-respect worthy of attention on the world stage. It is how the people of a country express their dreams and hopes, and how they talk about their past and their future. It is what they care about.
Culture is about the conservation and appreciation of the past, of our diverse backgrounds, of our heritage. But it is also about the future, about innovation and creation, the creative imagination of who we are and what we want to become.
We believe as Liberals that investment in the arts is an investment in Canada's future. It is a common language that binds and builds for a stronger Canadian society.
We believe that cultural endeavours contribute to what Edward Blake once so aptly described as the cultivation of the national spirit. We could certainly use a good dose of that building of national unity, of shared dreams across this land.
The Canadian vision is not new, but it is just with preserving, cultivating and promoting it which will bring the kind of nourishment and encouragement that is required. It seems to be absent from the leadership across the floor of this House.
I would like to say that Canada's cultural community's contribution to nourish the mind and the soul of its people has been diminished with the revelations of this government's budget and the unveiling of its Estimates. Canadians deserve better.
A recent Department of Communications working paper stated that the impact of vibrant cultural exploration, of striving for creative excellence on performance


March 8, 1990

in all forms of research, creative analysis and innovation is vital to Canada's competitiveness as a society.
We are also told by the Department of Communications that the cultural sector has out-performed most other sectors of the economy in the creation of jobs over the past two decades, and that Canadian cultural attractions have been recognized as powerful assets in the development of tourism.
The value of the economic activity created by cultural endeavours has also been recognized. This is an industry that grosses in excess of $9 billion and directly generates 150,000 jobs.
As well, the employment training and job creation aspects of the cultural sector are impressive. It is labour intensive. Its workforce is highly educated and mobile. The sector's strong contribution to tourism and economic development has resulted because of support reflected in federal, provincial and municipal policies and programs.
It is unfortunate that this government in its latest budget is not continuing that support. At a time when the strength of our cultural life is becoming more and more important and much more deeply appreciated to identify us as a very important and independent nation among the family of men, I find this government's pretence for the support an unconscionable smokescreen.
Just add the planned impact of the GST on this whole service sector-hotel bills, restaurants, taxis, theatres, movie houses, health and sports spas, country fairs, folk arts, museums, libraries, books and magazines. As people pay the tax on the stamp for the postcard they bought, to which the GST has been added, to write home, they are going to be writing: "Don't bother to come. Go elsewhere, otherwise you will be taxed from gas to food to entertainment. In fact, you will be taxed to death".
Any pretence that this government has a cultural policy was put to rest with the Wilson budget. The Conservatives once again took aim at the CBC with cuts of $20 million over the next two years to its capital equipment budget. This comes after $140 million in cuts
The Budget
and 500 in staff reductions. We will have to wait to see if the CBC will be able to continue to provide high quality delivery of programming, not to mention Canadian content.
I would remind you, Madam Speaker, that last night at the ACTRA Awards we saw cuts and clips from Switchback, one of the programs which was just recently cut.
Furthermore, the $13 million in freeze over the next two years to Telefilm, coming after the decimation of tax incentives for film and video productions, no film distribution bill and no film policy show that this government has no intention of building, let alone sustaining, a Canadian film industry.
This government has pulled the guts out of our most pervasive and cultural mediums-the film industry and public broadcasters. They are the instruments that shape the intellect and the imagination of Canadians, and we are not providing any Hollywood alternatives.
With respect to provincial and municipal spending, if you look at the figures of Statistics Canada, Madam Speaker, you will see that provincial governments spent a total of $1.34 billion on culture in 1986-1987, 60 per cent of which was financial aid to artists and cultural institutions. At the municipal level, municipal governments also sustain the arts. They spent a total of $774.8 million on arts and culture, which represents 17 per cent of total government expenditures at all levels.
With the cuts that are going forward in the federal-provincial transfer grants, there is the potential for a domino effect, and cuts in the fields of cultural production at both the provincial and municipal levels.
As well, an announcement by the President of the Treasury Board in December eliminating existing arrangements for municipalities on radio licence fees for mobile radios used in emergency services, such as ambulance, fire and police, as well as for public works and transit vehicles, increases their costs. Presently, the municipalities pay a flat fee of $236 for one base station and one mobile radio. For example, Orillia will now go up to $6,535. The city of Vancouver will pay $70,174-70 times more than its current budget.
I will tell you that if you have these kinds of increases for fire, ambulance and police, they will be pitted against support for the arts.

March 8, 1990
The Budget
I would like to conclude by saying that Canada's cultural life has been impacted negatively by this Conservative government. It will long remain one of the worse legacies to Canada, if you examine it across the centuries.

I think it would have been a good idea.
If he wants to withdraw a terrible broadcast bill now, I would be prepared to look at-

speechtext: You wrote half of it.

speechtext:
Don't faint! I wrote half of it. The half I wrote, I like. The half you did, I do not like.
Let us move on to Telesat. I would suggest to the hon. parliamentary secretary that there is a place in public policy for an integrated telephone and telecommunications system. It would be a telephone system that would be universally accessible and affordable. It is through the controls inherent in Telesat that we could ensure that.
With respect to the Radio Act, I would ask the hon. parliamentary secretary and the government to go back to look at the amendments and the arguments I brought forward. The second was the impact on municipalities. We saw the potential there during the course of dealing with that bill. I tried to bring forward an amendment. However, I received an assurance from the minister of the day, who is not the present minister, that the municipalities would not be impacted negatively. You can see how much that word was worth in today's market-place.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for Mount Royal for her presentation. Since today is International Women's Day, I wonder if she could talk a little about the cuts and how they are going to affect women in the field of communications.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wish there were more women involved in the broadcasting industry, in the CBC, at the National Film Board, in the infrastructure of those organizations which should be reporting under the concept of the Employment Equity Act. Unfortunately, we do not have enough women, as we do not have enough visible minorities, within these particular structures, whether it is private sector broadcasters and cable companies or the public sector broadcasters.
The employment equity bill, Bill C-62, passed through the House. That bill punishes a corporation if it does not deposit a plan of action, but it has no financial penalty within its purview. A positive step forward was not enacted. That is one of the reasons why the government
March 8, 1990

has not been effective in the promotion of women in the arts and culture scene.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to participate in the budget debate. I also had the privilege of speaking in the debate on the first budget of this government back in 1985. I was proud then of the steps taken by the government in that budget. I am proud of the fact that we have stayed on the course that we set for ourselves at that time. I am proud that today's budget continues in that tradition.
We have had to do a number of things, none of them, I am sure you would admit, Madam Speaker, are easy. We have had to restrain the growth of certain government programs. We have had to freeze others, reduce some and eliminate still others. But all of them are continuing Canada on the course that was set by the Minister of Finance in late 1984, that is, to tackle the deficit.
We have heard a lot of criticism from the members of the opposition. When I think of being a member of the opposition-and I have never had that experience-it seems to me it would be an easy job to do. They oppose all attempts to control government spending. They oppose all attempts to increase government revenues. To top it off, they propose nothing.
I take it that is a theory of theirs to regain popularity and to regain the government of this country. It did not work for them in 1984. They know it did not work for them in 1988. I am going to suggest to them again, and they can remember me saying this to them here, it is not going to work in 1992. Canadians want a government that is willing to take the kind of tough decisions that the Minister of Finance has been taking these past six years.
I would like to talk a little bit about some of the elements of this budget. One of them is the freeze on EPF, Established Programs Financing, which has been frozen for the next couple of years. I would like to speak specifically with respect to my home province of Ontario.
The first point I would like to make is that it is not that the federal government does not support provincial government services. We do. We believe provincial government services are important. In this budget alone
The Budget
we will contribute over $30 billion to the provinces to help out in the area of provincial concerns.
When we are trying at the federal level to deal with a deficit that is over $300 billion, certain questions have to be asked. Some of those questions are these. Who is in the best position to help out in the funding of provincial services? I can tell you that I know that the province of Ontario can help out.
Let us face the facts. For 43 years the province of Ontario had a Progressive Conservative government that managed this province very well. Since 1984, assisted by the policies of this government, there have had boom times in the province of Ontario. So is the province of Ontario able to help share the burden of providing provincial government services? I think it is.
I can tell you that we certainly got a boost the day before the budget. I noticed the provincial treasurer in Ontario-and I am reading from an article in The Globe and Mail of February 20-had just discovered $952 million in "unanticipated revenues". That was certainly a boost in sharing the burden of provincial services, one that I am sure all of us in this House appreciate at a time when the federal government is trying to come to grips with this difficult deficit.
Madam Speaker, you have heard in this Chamber on many occasions complaints from members of the Liberal party in particular. They complain about the Conservatives referring to the time when they were in office. You have heard it many times, and I heard it just recently on Tuesday afternoon. A Liberal member of Parliament was complaining. He said: "Why do the Tories always bring up what we did in government? Why do they always want to talk about the Liberal record? Why do they not talk about what they have done?"
I can tell them that I am very pleased to talk about the Conservative record, and I will talk about the Conservative record. I have always wondered where I heard that complaint before, that plea, that bleating not to talk about our record here. I remembered where it was. It was from the days before I was a member of Parliament when I was a legal aid duty counsel. I used to represent people on bail hearings. Very often the last thing in the world people who are up for bail wanted to have discussed in court was their record. If you had their record, many times they would say: "Well, that was so many years ago. Do we have to talk about what happened in the past?" That reminds me of the Liberal party. I can tell you, Madam Speaker, I am pleased at all times to talk about the Conservative record in 1984, 1985, 1986, right up to 1990. That is the difference between a Liberal

The Budget
and a Conservative. They do not want to talk about what they did in government because they are ashamed of their record.
On the subject of the Liberal record, let us talk about it a little bit. When we took office in 1984 the deficit was over $200 billion. Just the interest on that $200 billion is now $120 billion. So we have $320 billion of debt left to us by the Liberal party. If members of that party want to know how long I am going to talk about it, I will talk about that Liberal debt until it is paid off by our children and grandchildren. That is the length of time that Canadians should remember, and remember after that if they ever consider voting Liberal again. That is how long they should remember that debt. We are still waiting for those Liberal party solutions to this problem.
I was interested to hear that the former Liberal Prime Minister of this country is coming out with a book. I am sure it will be very helpful to the discussions going on in Canada today.
I am going to tell you about the chapter I want to see. If the former Prime Minister of this country, Mr. Trudeau, has so many great ideas as to what this government should be doing, I want to hear what he has to say about the deficit. He and his policies created that $200 billion deficit that has grown to $320 billion. I think it is reasonable to hear what he has to say in terms of being helpful in solving this problem that we all face.
I think that Canadians can accept the directions that have been taken by the Minister of Finance. When people point out to me that we are down in the polls I always say to them: "You don't change economic policy in this country on a month-to-month basis depending on what the polls say".
As well, I tell them that if irresponsible spending would keep you in power, if spending money that you do not have, if spending money that you have to borrow would have kept anybody in power the Liberals would have been in power in a one-party democracy forever.
But it did not work for them, and it is not going to work again in the future.
When I talk about Liberal spending-and I love to do it-I am reminded of so many examples in my area of the Niagara Peninsula. I remember for instance one woman telling me after I was elected: "You know we had a project here, a very worth-while project. We received a cheque from the government and we didn't even ask for it. We hadn't even applied and it arrived in the mail". I said to her: "You know as worth while as some of these things are I can tell you, Ma'am, that the days of spending money, of passing out money without people even asking for it are unfortunately coming to an end".
I see I have only a couple of minutes left. I can tell this House for the benefit of some hon. members in the Liberal party who question whether the Conservative party is behind the Minister of Finance that the members of this party are behind the Minister of Finance. They are behind the policies that he has taken in 1990, just as we have been behind him since 1984. Not only is that good for the Conservative party and is going to keep this party in government, we know it is good for Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am delighted to hear the hon. parliamentary secretary make a fire and brimstone speech in trying to fire up the troops. I can understand they need it when their riding associations are being taken over by anti-GST forces that want to force out the members of this House on the Conservative side who are voting for this silly legislation. They are trying to fire their members out; they want to replace them. I can understand his nervousness and his attempt to fire up the troops and say that the members are all behind this bill because they know they are going to pay a price for supporting this budget and supporting the disastrous policies that this government has instituted over the last five years, policies that have cost the Canadian people billions, and the hon. member knows that.
The hon. member talks about his anxiety to discuss Conservative policies and his willingness to defend the record of incompetence for the last five years. Would he discuss with the House the level of tax increases that we have had? Would he produce the figures on the addition-

al revenue that this government has gouged out of the Canadian public in five years of economic mismanagement and compare the amount it has taken from the people with the size of the deficit?
Let us examine what it has called budget reduction. We keep hearing, and I have heard it at least three times during the course of this debate, that 70 per cent of the cutbacks in the deficit are a result of cuts in government spending. I would like to hear how much of it in fact was the result of increases in taxation which the Conservatives have gouged out of the Canadian people. That is the figure we should be looking at in this House. That is the figure the hon. parliamentary secretary should be referring to. I invite him to come up with those figures now. Perhaps he does not have them.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to respond to the member who raised the subject of tax increases. He specifically referred to the GST and challenged me to defend Tory tax increases.
I can tell the hon. member, I do not shy away from them at all. I have said here that there are cuts in government spending, there is restraint in growth in government spending, there have been changes in tax and there have been tax increases in the last five or six years. I have been pleased to defend them because I know it puts Canada on the right track.
I was at an all-candidates debate in the 1988 election and somebody thought they would pin me down by asking: "How could you have gotten rid of the home ownership savings plan? What possible reason could you have?". I said: "It is for the money. The federal government is in financial difficulty. " That is why we have had to overhaul the tax system. That is why we have had to make cuts in government spending, because we know it is necessary.
Now the hon. member talked about the GST. I am going to tell you something. I was more than passing interested in the debates the other night between the Minister of Finance and the Liberal critic on the subject of finance of the GST. I love to look at newspaper articles and certainly to see newspaper articles from the province of Alberta. Just let me give a few examples of what they were saying in Alberta after the finance critic from the Liberal party spoke. One of the editorials in the
The Budget
Edmonton Sun stated: "No new ideas". It was referring to the Liberals. "No new ideas".
The Edmonton Journal states: "A Grit's empty promise". That is what is thought about the Liberal finance policies here. The Edmonton Sun referring to the Minister of Finance, "Mr. Cool should be happy". It says: "Liberal hedges debate pledge. Wilson's leadership shone in GST clash".
In the Globe and Mail: "Confusion increasing over Liberal GST stand". Why should that be any different than anything else? Why should it be any different than the Liberal Party on Meech Lake or free trade or deficit reduction? That is just par for the course. But I will be fair, maybe the Liberals are just confused about the big ticket items. We are behind the Minister of Finance. Maybe the Liberal critic should talk to his colleagues and figure out where they stand on the GST.
The Globe and Mail got it right. I would be glad to table this if any of the hon. members would like me to. Certainly I would be pleased to send this out to any of my constituents.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, last week, since the House was not sitting, I took advantage of this opportunity to talk to my constituents in Outremont.
I wanted to know more about their concerns, their expectations and their problems. Although age and interests vary, on the whole, the people of Outremont are concerned about the environment, income stability, interest rates, employment, immigration and the future of their community.
I also heard some comments, not always veiy favourable, on the Budget brought down on February 20 by the Minister of Finance Although not everyone was satisfied with the Budget, all the people I talked to saw the Budget and the minister's agenda as an expression of the government's will to provide even more efficient management and to bring the deficit and our national debt under control.

The Budget
Madam Speaker, this is the Progressive Conservative Government's sixth Budget, and once again, it reflects the government's thoroughly consistent and serious approach to meeting its objectives. It is the culmination of five years of hard work during which the government has reviewed and updated regulatory procedures, revamped our tax system by lowering tax rates and eliminating loopholes, abolished trade barriers, improved manpower training programs and turned around the country's economic situation.
Despite gloomy forecasts, over 1.5 million jobs were created since the beginning of our term, and among the major industrial countries, only Japan's economic performance outshipped ours. However, to provide for an even more prosperous future, we must eliminate our deficit and reduce the debt, making Canadians less vulnerable to the impact of interest rates and to inflation which is a threat to us all. They will feel more secure and will be able to operate even more effectively.
We must act now, in a manner that is both effective and compassionate, to control our debt while maintaining the programs and services we cherish. This is the only way we can preserve a climate conducive to maintaining our economic, social and psychological development.
To act now, Madam Speaker, means ensuring that the electorate, the citizens of Canada, become even more aware of their important role in determining the future of their country and our society.
Previous Liberal governments encouraged Canadians to depend on government and often forced them to do so. After the war, the central government was given a mandate to help the country and its citizens recover from a situation that had destabilized the economy. We had to reconvert from a wartime to a peacetime economy. This position was sound because we had a vigorous economic recovery. The reconversion went well. However, instead of letting Canadians continue to become more dynamic, the government decided to keep on exercising power by controlling the economic levers rather than trusting Canadians. It wanted to keep the leading role and increase the process of centralization, thereby keeping the spotlight on its supposedly brilliant performance.
Under Mr. Trudeau, who claimed to have contempt for nationalists, the government and he showed a distrustful nationalism towards the Americans and the obvious differences among the provinces. This mistrust resulted in undue control and supervision, as with the Foreign Investment Review Agency; the nationalization of several industries could only lead to increased dependence.
He succeeded in developing passive behaviour and discouraging, if not killing, creativity and innovation. Everywhere people showed "sweet indifference".
We reached the point, Madam Speaker, where someone who was thinking of starting a new project would first find out what grant programs were available. By repeating that people had rights, we made them forget that they also had duties and resources. We were depriving them of the pride that comes from doing something oneself. We were preparing poorly for future challenges.
We all know that in a competitive world like today's, only the most inventive and most able to benefit from their environment can win.
Experts think that the latest Budget is reasonable, courageous and responsible.
Bernard Landry, the former PQ Finance Minister, described it as a very good budget. He even said that, under the circumstances, it was a tremendous achievement.
Personally, I suggest that this budget opens an era of individual initiative enhancement. It emphasizes the responsibility of institutions, groups and individuals. It is a perfect tool which will allow Canadians to build up their self-esteam based on their own achievements.
Needless to say, the Government will continue to help the most destitute regain their self-sufficiency, increase their awareness of their self-worth while relying if need be on Government programs and services.
Like all the other Members of this House, we, of the Quebec caucus, have emphasized the areas where the Government could continue to improve its administrative efficiency and we shall continue to work toward the implementation of spending restraint.
Finally, the Government will especially seek to improve further the productivity of the governmental process by working toward a closer relationship with the
March 8, 1990

Public Service. We carry out a very careful selection of Government employees and we are anxious to hire the best candidates. By encouraging a climate more conducive to dialogue in the face of a common objective, our Government will successfully reach its goal which is to ensure future generations a superior quality of life.
Madam Speaker, you will note that I am not referring to figures as such. I feel that this Budget is as much, if not more a reflection of a management philosophy as an ideological position.
As a matter of fact, Madam Speaker, I have stated before in this House that culture comes before economy. From such a statement stems also the fact that a realistic budget must reflect reality as closely as possible. If it is true that a person could not mortgage his or her health with impunity, it is also true that a society could not indefinitely mortage its future. A balance must be achieved. All individuals must put their psychosomatic portfolios in order. Human nature has its needs which no one can disregard.
The Canadian society had reached the point of no return. The machine was starting to overload as a reaction to the consecutive budgets which, before 1984, had resulted from unrealistic expectations, as if the country would never reach the bottom of the barrel, as if there would be no end to growth for growth's sake.
Well, the Canadian people, in their wisdom, have asked this Progressive Conservative Government to stop this hemorrhage. But for a great many years the Minister had to live with past commitments and deal with the law of inertia. Before a crisis, is upon us the minister did talk a Budget which will put an end to this downtrend and put us on the road to recovery.
Madam Speaker, although the Budget may seem tough, the Canadian people generally want it. It is a common sense budget we should all be proud of.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for the opportunity to ask him some questions which might help me clarify a few points for the benefit of my constituents. I have the feeling that I drew the attention of all members of the House the day I rose to ask for a grant on behalf of the Missing Children network. Six-odd months later they finally did get a grant for three
The Budget
jobs, I believe. Jobs, jobs, jobs and the creation of many jobs are issues we often hear about in the House. I do not recollect the exact figures because I think they are not quite correct. When I talk about three jobs in my riding I am referring to three part-time jobs, and that works out to only one job over a 12-month employment period. Would the hon. member for Outremont explain how he can boast about creating so many new openings when in most instances these are really part-time jobs? We might get a more realistic figure if we were to divide by three.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The question of my opposition colleague raises an interesting and important issue. Indeed it is a basic issue, and all members of the House and all Canadians, I would suggest, have to take a stand and endeavour to find the most acceptable solutions to such a wide-ranging issue. Surely my colleague does not expect me to play the role of the various ministers who have the mandate, the responsibility and, perforce, the wide array of knowledge to respond specifically to such a question. As I understand the question, it has to involve more than three part-time jobs in the riding of Saint-Laurent-Cartierville because the same thing happens in the riding I represent, just as it does elsewhere across Canada. Indeed, similar concerns and questions are raised in the various university faculties where applications for scholarships or labour income support cannot all be fully entertained.
I conclude therefore that the question of my colleague raises a broader issue. This is why at the end of my remarks I said it was a question of-I will not use the word ideology-but a question of philosophy. Either we decide to centralize even more and, willy-nilly, the people will identify with a process of dependency. This wall-to-wall theory did prevail in Quebec over a number of years. We even saw a Quebec Finance Minister who, after having favoured this wall-to-wall program approach for some time, decided that there was a price to pay for always expecting the federal and provincial governments to have enough money. This redistributed money must come not only from the pockets of Canadian citizens but also from the work they get paid for. Part of their pay is taxed by the government and returned to them as services. This distributive justice operates across the country.

March 8, 1990
The Budget
To conclude, in answer to your question, I repeat: it is a matter of philosophy. The Minister of Finance and the Progressive Conservative Party have more faith in decentralization and believe that individual drive combined with group dynamics will increase production. The return on investment is bigger than with centralization, as we experienced it, fortunately or unfortunately, under the Liberal government of Mr. Trudeau, which made our population more dependent and more passive and led to less creativity and innovation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this year's budget will be remembered as a budget of half truths and deviousness. It is a nearsighted budget without any vision of the future, a budget that hurts the under-privileged and that does not even try to avoid the impending recession.
The Minister of Finance claims the deficit is now under control. Can we believe him? Since this Tory Government was first elected in September 1984 the national debt increased twofold from $170 billion to the current $350 billion.
The Tories' mismanagement of the economy is reflected in the somber outlook for the current fiscal year. Unemployment inflation, and interest rates will jump up and international financial markets have lost confidence in our dollar.
We are verging on recession, yet the Minister of Finance suggests we should not try and avoid it.
The minister claims there is no new taxes. He simply passed on to the provinces an $8 billion debt. And certainly the GST will be the worst tax grab in Canadian history.
The minister claims that deficit reduction is not harming social programs. But he is cutting health care and social welfare. Social housing funding is cut $165 million over five years, making more serious the situation of the 200,000 homeless Canadians and all those spending more than half of their income on rent.
To cap it all, the minister claims the budget is fair. But regional development assistance is cancelled for all practical purposes, as the Americans wanted.
More than 5,000 veterans under palliative care because of old age will have to pay more than $3,000 each
for their hospital beds. Natives once more are the target of budget cuts. Official Development Assistance once more is cut. At the same time, large corporations are getting govemement tax handouts while defence expenditure, still at a high level, do not reflect the new world political situation.
The budget tabled by the Minister of Finance is unfair and near-sighted. It ignores today's economic problems and includes no agenda for the new decade.

I want to continue by looking at the budget in some detail. As the co-critic for forestry for my party, I think it is important that we look at the forestry sector as well. To do that, I want first to quote from the Minister of Forestry on the establishment of the new forestry department. I think it is a credit to the government and to all parties here that we passed such a motion in the House to develop such a department.
The minister states in his communique: "The creation of the department is an acknowledgement of the government's firm commitment to our forests". That sounds good. The words are nice, but the record shows that in the government's budget last year, the one that was supposed to be committed to forestry, it cut the forestry department's budget by 11.9 per cent. This was a new department cut by 11.9 per cent.
This year, funding has been cut by $47.6 million from $206.9 million, which is a reduction to the total of $159.3 million. If we look at the forecasted expenditures of $231.4 million, the reduction is 31 per cent, a reduction of $72.1 million. One wonders where that commitment is. Words are nice, but the action is not there.
If we examine the forestry department closer and look at the agreements, I must say that the government was wise in renewing the forestry agreements in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. That is a positive step in the right direction. There is nothing wrong with that. However, there are four other provinces whose agreements expired last year, namely, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. What is the government waiting for?
This year agreements will expire with Newfoundland, Quebec and British Columbia. The Estimates will show that there is no money put aside for any new agreements. We must wonder what type of commitment this govern-
March 8, 1990

ment is sold to, or whether it is just going to give us some words?
The minister stated in his budget tabled in the House on February 20 that there will be no new taxes. It is hard to believe. When we look little further into the budget, it deals with says something along the lines of sales tax reform. It also has: "The Impact of the GST". I find it hard to believe that he would say that there are no new taxes. We. never had a GST before. The government plans on implementing it in this fiscal year, and it says that there are no new taxes.
When we add to that the cuts to the transfer payments to the provinces, there will be tax increases. If there are not there are certainly going to be program cuts, so it is hard to believe that someone could say that there will be no new taxes.
While I am on the point of taxes I would like to read a paragraph from the Liberal minority report that summarizes my thoughts on the GST quite plainly. "The GST proposal would create economic disruption, increase taxes on average families, introduce an unprecedented level of complexity into the tax system, impose further hardship on low income Canadians, remain hidden from taxpayers, shift the tax burden in several important ways in Canadian society without the government fully understanding the long term effects of the shifts, cause financial difficulties for provincial governments and harm many sectors of the Canadian economy." Anyone wishing a copy of that quotation may contact my office. But that sums up what the Liberal Party feels about this GST. It also sums up what most small businesses and most people in Canada feel about it.
When we were in government we talked about fairness too, but at least our words meant something. We were fair. At least we attempted to be fair. Let us look at the budget document a little more closely and study the revenue table. The parliamentary secretary a while ago was talking about the Conservative record and how proud he was of it. Let's look at that record.
When the Conservatives took over in 1984, the percentage of personal income tax revenue was at 41.3 per cent. In other words, the government received 41.3 per cent of its revenue from individuals through income tax. In 1988-89, that figure, lo and behold, is up to 44.3 per cent and rising. But if we look at the corporate sector, in
The Budget
1984 the percentage it paid was 13.2 per cent and now-it is hard to believe-that percentage is down to 11.3 per cent. Individuals are paying more and corporations are paying less. It does not seem to gibe with fairness.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I too would like to take part part today in this budget debate on the last budget which the Minister of Finance has just submitted.
I want to do so in the context of a province that has not yet fully recovered from the last budget, the one that we had in 1989. My province certainly well remembers the last budget because it dealt such a blow to the people of Summerside, in fact to all Islanders, when it was announced that CFB Summerside would be closed.
As Islanders, we have a special pride in the quality of life that exists in our province. Our predominantly rural outlook allows us to maintain a sense of community and unique values which cannot exist within an urban environment. Prince Edward Island has often been called the million acre farm because rural activities flourish from one end of our Island to the other.
We are very proud of our lifestyle, but I can tell you that we certainly are concerned with the government's policies which consistently erode rural life in our province.
We were very proud of Canadian Forces Base Summerside and proud to be part of Canada's national defence program. Last year, the budget really devastated Prince Edward Island with its arbitrary decision to close CFB Summerside. Today, on March 8, practically a year later, we still do not have any firm commitment from the government.
I have addressed the House many times on the issue of CFB Summerside. The government has to come to terms with the enormity of its decision to close the base, and it has to take responsibility for that decision.
The loss of this base has caused severe hardship, economically, socially and emotionally, in Summerside and the whole surrounding area. The government has been asked time and time again to take responsibility for the decision to close the base, and yet the federal government refuses to listen.
March 8, 1990

A budget has been brought down and still it contains no special help for the people affected by the closure of CFB Summerside. This closure announced last April would cost the area approximately 1,200 direct jobs, an annual payroll of approximately $40 million, or more than 2 per cent of the total provincial economy. Certainly our pride as Islanders has not diminished, but our faith has been shattered.
The government's 1990 budget contains measures which will certainly cost Prince Edward Island millions of dollars. The largest cut will come from the money that we will be losing under Established Programs Financing. My province will lose approximately $35 million in five years and about $12 million to $13 million within the next two.
The federal government started cutting these payments back in 1986. The cuts up to 1990 were to have totalled $11 million, but now on top of that we have another $12 million to $13 million, and that is all within two years.
In his budget speech the finance minister spoke about building a secure and rewarding foundation on a solid foundation. That foundation is education, but the government has been eroding that foundation persistently since it came to office and it has truly put this country's future at risk. This policy error is even more serious for a province like Prince Edward Island which needs a well trained workforce to lead it into the 1990s and beyond and to self-sufficiency. With continual cuts to education and the neglect of the Canada Student Loans Program, Ottawa is condemning my province to a future of dependency on the federal government. It is bad policy, it is bad economics, and it is bad for Prince Edward Islanders.
This budget also contains a reduction to Marine Atlantic's operating subsidy of approximately $9 million over a two-year period. This is only the most recent cut for this Crown corporation. Since 1985 the government has effectively reduced Marine Atlantic's subsidy by $52 million. Now 37 per cent of the cost of operation for Marine Atlantic comes from the users of the system, so 63 per cent comes from government subsidy. Here again this subsidy is being reduced. That means that Marine Atlantic will have to cut services, cut expenses, or increase fares. Only time will tell whether rates will have to be increased again.
The Budget
The list of program cuts which affect my province and therefore impact on our economy is lengthy. There is the cancellation of the Postal Services Review Board. This comes at a time when Canadians need a forum to voice their concerns about Canada Post. Certainly across Prince Edward Island many Islanders are upset with Canada Post's policy to close rural post offices. This review board provided an independent body to keep an eye on the state of the postal service in Canada.
Another aspect of its mandate was to help Canada Post achieve its objectives. It certainly leaves the question: what is Canada Post's objective? Here again, it convinces Islanders that the government is eroding our rural lifestyle.
The cut in funding to the Veterans Independence Program is yet another example of where the government places its responsibilities. It plans to streamline this whole program. It is going to cut $18 million out of the program, and that is money that could provide a great deal of care and assistance for those in need.
The intent of this program is to assist veterans in maintaining or improving their quality of life by helping them remain healthy and independent. Without proper funding this program cannot provide the necessary services to veterans who so willingly provided their services. As Canadians we owe a great debt to our veterans and certainly they deserve to be treated fairly. In my province we have close to 1,200 veterans who are in need of the Veterans Independence Program, and approximately 200 of them live in my riding of Malpeque.
The list continues with cuts to programs under the Department of National Health and Welfare. The loss of funding to this department will also contribute to the undermining of the quality of life of Prince Edward Island.
I see that my time is running out. I have a great deal more to say about this budget, and certainly I will be speaking at a later time in the House.

Government members get up to make speeches and extenuating statements which do not give the member who made his speech a chance to reply. I think that is unfair.
Possibly we should refer this whole question back to a committee of the House so we can come up with an answer to the problem which has been with us for the last while. Indeed questions and comments have to be short questions and short comments. Otherwise, the whole process of making a debate in this House is
March 8, 1990

becoming a monologue for the government to put its propaganda on the record, and I object to that.

speechtext: Sounds great!

speechtext:
Yes, it does, and this reminds me of the upcoming press conference with your former prime minister on March 20. He says-the press is already reporting his comments-that the Free Trade Agreement is a worse threat to our sovereignty.
Speaking of the Americans, I will try to be objective about this. According to an American sociologist, the Constitution of 1982 is a worse threat to Canadian sovereignty. Not the Constitution as such but the fact that we enshrined the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. When we compare American and Canadian institutions, we see that here in Canada, with its Anglo-Saxon tradition in our institutions, here in the House of Commons, for instance, we have a collective hierarchy where rights and privileges are given collectively. In the United States they have the Bill of Rights and the emphasis is on amendments and individual claims. In this particular area, however, Canadians have been assimilated to a far greater extent. Taking a closer look at the Machiavellian schemes of your former prime minister, his purpose in enshrining the Charter was to direct challenges against Quebec's Bill 101.
Madam Speaker, that being said, what damaged our sovereignty most is the deplorable state in which the economy was left by the Liberal Party in 1984.
As I said to the hon. member for Restigouche-Cha-leur, remember that in 1968, because history is important-To plan for the future, we must understand the past. In 1968, a hundred years after Confederation, our national debt was $18 billion. No annual deficit. No constitutional problems. Everybody was part of the constitutional family. The country was in fine fettle. At the time, we were paying 12 cents on every tax dollar to service the debt and we even had enough to pay back part off part of the capital. After 1968, the first time the Liberal Government incurred a deficit was in 1975. Five years later, in 1980, we had a record annual deficit of $11.5 billion. From 1980 to 1984, the previous government went from bad to worse. No cutbacks, certainly not! It increased government spending at an average rate of 15.1 per cent annually, when it already had a deficit of $11.5 billion in 1980. Since 1984, we have managed to bring this average rate down to 5.2 per cent.

March 8, 1990
The Budget
What is even more astonishing, Madam Speaker, is that if we do not include the cost of servicing the debt, the previous government increased program spending at an average rate of 13.9 per cent, and this was only for its operating budget. All those election goodies were part of the 13.9 per cent. Since 1984, however, we have managed to keep increases in program spending down to an average of 3.5 per cent. This year, the increase will be only 3 per cent, well below the rate of inflation.
From $11.5 billion in 1980, the annual deficit grew to $38.3 billion in 1984. This was too much for Canadians. After 100 years we had a deficit of $18 billion. In 1984, it was up to $38.3 billion. When we consider the operating budget alone, without the cost of servicing the debt, it is a real disaster. The operating budget indicates what the government collects in the form of taxes and income tax, and what it spends.
In 1984, the operating budget plus interest charges amounted to a deficit of $38.3 billion, but the operating budget alone showed a deficit of $16 billion.
In 1989-90, we turned this operating deficit of $16 billion into an operating surplus of more than $9 billion, and in fact we did this two years in a row. In the 1990 Budget we are forecasting a surplus of $13 billion for next year's operating budget. Granted, we still have a deficit of $30.5 billion. It is simple arithmetic. With the debt you left us in 1984, and this was $38.5 billion annually, a cumulative $200 billion since 1975-imagine, in ten years, less than ten years, $200 billion worth of debt! If we consider our present debt, $350 billion, $120 billion of that goes to service it, so over the past five years, 80 per cent of our debt consisted of the cost of servicing it. How can you accuse us of doubling the debt when today, Canadians are not really getting their money's worth, because they are paying the bill in tax dollars, and besides, we have an operating surplus of over $9 billion. I don't know whether you are good at arithmetic, but we mentioned earlier what percentage of the debt actually consists of interest charges.
Can you imagine, we would need a budget surplus in excess of $40 billion! And if ever we reached that level the deficit by then would be well over $600 or $700 billion! You have not even an inkling of the predicament your government left us in, yet today you have the nerve to tell us we doubled the deficit. As a matter of fact we
will double it again in the next few years because, if you attended school long enough, you must have learned that we operate in a compound-interest environment. As if this were not enough, remember that when we attempted to reduce some programs-like de-indexing old age pensions-we were faced with endless protests, parades and demonstrations accusing us of being heartless slashers. You never did co-operate-
